name: Thailand
summary_text: The Immigration Bureau runs 'Welcome Pride by Immigration', launched on 5 August 2024, which addresses the concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports do not match their current appearance or gender and eases immigration scrutiny on arrival. It is the one entry-side accommodation a trans visitor can rely on before landing.  Same-sex marriage has been legal since 22 January 2025, after the bill passed its final Senate reading in June 2024, making Thailand the first country in Southeast Asia to do so; the statute uses gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms. Couples who married after that date gain access to property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims from which they were previously excluded.  Legal gender recognition remains absent. There is no mechanism to change the sex marker on a birth certificate, national ID card or passport, and official title prefixes are fixed to the sex recorded at birth, so a trans woman's documents may still carry a male honorific. The Name Act 1962 offers only a partial workaround through first-name change, and even that leaves final discretion with officials. A 2021 Human Rights Watch report, 'People Can't Be Fit into Boxes', documented the absence of any route to documentation reflecting gender identity and found that anti-discrimination protections are not fully enforced. Anti-discrimination law has existed since 2015. At a 2025 'Pride in Action' forum at Lido Connect, advocates urged the government to expedite a gender-recognition law after marriage equality, confirming that recognition legislation was still pending.  Thai law carries no hate-crime designation. In April 2025 a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya after she refused his request for sex; the perpetrator was named in domestic reporting as 42-year-old Fu Tongyung. The community described the killing as a hate crime, but bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as an ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties and no collection of bias-crime data, and LGBTQ+ groups subsequently called for new hate-crime protections. The gap is an accountability problem a trans visitor should weigh when assessing how a violent incident involving them would be classified.  Detention carries documented risk. The Department of Corrections states that LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993, and at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; of roughly 300,000 Thai prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities. Trans woman Theerayut Charoenpakdee, stopped by police in 2017 and expecting to be held with men because her documents still carried the title 'Mr.', was instead placed in the separated wing. The pattern is uneven: trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request, where officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and where she was harassed at intake and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility; activists insisted placement should be an option rather than an obligation and warned that segregation could encourage exclusion. Reporting from 2016 also noted that transgender women outside such units usually face a choice between men's cells and solitary confinement.

sources.title: Penal Code Amendment Act of 1997 (No. 14) B.E. 2540
sources.documents: Decriminalization context and equal age of consent; set age of consent at fifteen years regardless of gender or sexual orientation following 1956 decriminalization of private adult consensual non-commercial sodomy
sources.detail: Cited as Penal Code Amendment Act of 1997 (Thai: พระราชบัญญัติแก้ไขเพิ่มเติมประมวลกฎหมายอาญา-(ฉบับที่-14)-พ.ศ.-2540). No URL visible in provided text.

sources.title: UNDP 2019 survey on LGBTQ discrimination in Thailand
sources.documents: Documents verbal harassment (53%), sexual assault (16%), pretending to be straight (42%), family discrimination (47.5%), suicidal ideation (49%) and attempts (17%); trans women highest levels - 61% verbal abuse, 22% sexual assault, 11% physical abuse, 8% police harassment, 32% workplace discrimination
sources.detail: Cited as 2019 UNDP survey/report; also notes only 44% of LGBTQ respondents knew about Gender Equality Act vs 50% non-LGBTQ. No URL visible in provided text.

name: Timor-Leste
summary_text: Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex sexual conduct. Same-sex sexual acts have been legal since 1975, and no source records anti-trans legislation, arrest patterns, or police targeting of trans people in the country. No law restricting trans people from public facilities, health care, or employment is documented.  No legal gender recognition procedure exists in Timor-Leste. For a visitor, the operative document is therefore the passport or identity card issued in the home jurisdiction, including any gender marker changed there. There is no domestic route by which a foreign trans person could alter or regularise a marker while in the country.  Official signals run in a supportive direction at the highest level. The Prime Minister gave televised endorsement to the country's first Pride parade in 2017, and President Francisco Guterres publicly backed the 2019 march, stating that he is a president for all people. Day-to-day rejection is nonetheless documented alongside those statements, including hostile messages sent to the family of a Pride organiser, so public visibility attracts both state endorsement and social hostility.  Pride marches are held annually in Dili, in July. A visitor present during those weeks can expect a visible public event of a scale that has grown substantially since 2017.

sources.title: Civil Code, Law No. 10/2011 - Articles 1467, 1517, 1858
sources.documents: Defines marriage as contract between two people of different sex; declares same-sex marriage legally non-existent; sets adoption eligibility tied to marriage, limiting same-sex couple adoption.
sources.detail: Cited in text as 'Civil Code (Law No. 10/2011)' Articles 1467 (Notion of marriage), 1517 (Non-existent marriages), 1858 (Who can adopt). No URL visible in text.
